common_name: Desert Pastel Autumn Sage (Pale Apricot Salvia greggii)

planting.note: Plant container plants in spring in lean, sharply drained soil in full sun; this selection is somewhat less cold-hardy than typical greggii cultivars and does best where winters stay mild.

directions: Desert Pastel is a Salvia greggii selection valued for its unusual pale apricot flowers brushed with faint yellow streaks, a softer, warmer tone than the reds and magentas typical of the species. It forms a compact, rounded subshrub that flowers from spring through fall and remains a steady draw for hummingbirds despite its muted color. Because it is less robust in hard winter cold than many greggii cultivars, give it a sheltered, sharply drained site and avoid exposed, wind-prone locations. A hard cutback in late winter keeps growth dense and encourages the heaviest flowering the following season.

common_name: Strawberries and Cream Autumn Sage (Pink-and-Yellow Bicolor Salvia greggii)

planting.note: Plant container plants in spring in well-drained to dry soil in full sun; this bicolor selection shows its creamy-yellow and pink tones best with consistent sun exposure.

directions: Strawberries and Cream is a Salvia greggii cultivar named for its distinctive bicolor flowers, which combine soft creamy-yellow tubes with pink-flushed lips rather than the solid reds or magentas common in the species. It forms a tidy, well-branched mound of aromatic gray-green foliage and flowers heavily from spring into fall, drawing hummingbirds and bees throughout. It shares the excellent heat and drought tolerance typical of autumn sage, needing only occasional deep watering once established. Trim lightly after each bloom flush to keep the plant compact and encourage repeat flowering.

common_name: Ribambelle Baby Sage (AGM Salmon-Pink Salvia microphylla)

planting.note: Root semi-hardwood cuttings in late summer or set out container plants in spring, in well-drained, average to lean soil in full sun.

directions: Ribambelle, a French name evoking a crowd or profusion, is a Salvia microphylla selection that holds the Royal Horticultural Society's Award of Garden Merit for its exceptionally heavy production of salmon-pink flowers from summer into fall. It forms a bushy, well-branched mound of aromatic foliage and ranks among the most floriferous microphylla cultivars, attracting hummingbirds and bees steadily through its long season. Established plants handle heat and drought well, needing supplemental water only in extended dry spells. Cut back hard to 6-12 inches in late winter to renew dense, floriferous growth.

common_name: James Compton Baby Sage (Dark Crimson Salvia microphylla)

planting.note: Root semi-hardwood cuttings in late summer or set out container plants in spring, in well-drained, average to lean soil in full sun.

directions: James Compton is a Salvia microphylla selection named for the English plant collector, distinguished by broad, oval, distinctly serrated leaves and large, dark crimson flowers that read noticeably deeper than the brighter scarlets of most microphylla cultivars. It forms an upright, well-branched shrub blooming from summer into fall and is a reliable hummingbird and bee plant through its long season. Like its parent species it is heat- and drought-tolerant once established, needing minimal supplemental water on lean, well-drained soil. A hard cutback to 6-12 inches in late winter renews dense growth and maximizes the following season's bloom.

common_name: Hoja Grande Baby Sage (Large-Leaved Magenta-Red Salvia microphylla)

planting.note: Root semi-hardwood cuttings in late summer or set out container plants in spring, in well-drained, average to lean soil in full sun.

directions: Hoja Grande, Spanish for 'big leaf', is a Salvia microphylla selection noted for foliage distinctly larger and darker green than typical microphylla cultivars, topped with magenta-red flowers from summer into fall. The oversized leaves give the plant a lusher, bolder look in the border than most baby sage selections, while the flower display still draws hummingbirds and bees heavily. It forms a vigorous, spreading mound that tolerates heat and drought well once established. Cut back hard to 6-12 inches in late winter to keep growth dense and encourage strong rebloom.

common_name: Trelissick Baby Sage (Creamy Yellow Salvia microphylla)

planting.note: Root semi-hardwood cuttings in late summer or set out container plants in spring, in well-drained, average to lean soil in full sun.

directions: Trelissick, named for the Cornish garden where this English-raised Salvia microphylla selection was developed, bears unusual creamy-yellow flowers on an upright, well-branched, aromatic shrub from summer into fall. The pale color sets it apart from the reds, pinks, and magentas that dominate most microphylla cultivars and makes it a useful foil for brighter companions in mixed plantings. It draws hummingbirds and bees steadily through its long bloom season and tolerates heat and drought well once established. Cut back hard to 6-12 inches in late winter to renew dense, upright growth.

common_name: Oxford Baby Sage (Dark Pink Salvia microphylla)

planting.note: Root semi-hardwood cuttings in late summer or set out container plants in spring, in well-drained, average to lean soil in full sun.

directions: Oxford is a Salvia microphylla selection grown for its saturated dark pink, two-lipped flowers on a bushy, well-branched mound of aromatic foliage, blooming from summer well into fall. It is a consistent hummingbird and bee plant through its long season and holds its deep color better in cooler fall weather than it does during peak summer heat. Established plants are heat- and drought-tolerant, needing supplemental water only during prolonged dry spells. Cut back hard to 6-12 inches in late winter to renew dense, floriferous growth.
